# Parasitic worms (hookworm, roundworm, tapeworm, guinea worm) (`parasitic_worms`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by sanitation_sewerage, food_hygiene, microscope, spontaneous_generation_refuted
- Core idea: Worms in the body do not arise there; each comes from eggs or larvae that entered by a known door. Hookworm larvae hatch in soil fouled with excrement and bore through bare feet, causing the pale, weak, 'lazy' sickness of warm farming country: latrines and shoes end it. Roundworm and whipworm eggs are swallowed with soil, unwashed vegetables and dirty fingers. Beef and pork can transmit different tapeworms; pork and wild game can carry Trichinella. Meat colour alone cannot establish a safe cooking temperature. Guinea worm comes from swallowing tiny water fleas: strain drinking water through tightly woven cloth and keep people with an emerging worm out of the pond. Blood flukes enter the skin when wading in still water with snails.
- Pitfalls:
  - Believing worms are generated by rotting food, bad humours or sweets inside the gut
  - Purging the worms out while people go on walking barefoot on fouled ground
  - Assuming smoking, salting or brief frying makes pork safe
  - Thinking this is only a tropical problem; medieval and Roman European latrines are full of worm eggs
- History: egypt: c. 1550 BC – Ebers papyrus describes worms and remedies; blood-fluke eggs found in mummies; 1851 Bilharz discovers the blood fluke in Cairo; 1898 Looss shows hookworm larvae enter through the skin; china: c. 168 BC – body of Lady Dai (Mawangdui) contains whipworm, pinworm and blood-fluke eggs; islamic: 1025 – Ibn Sina's Canon distinguishes several kinds of intestinal worm; europe: 1668–1684 – Redi shows parasites come from eggs; 1855 Küchenmeister demonstrates the tapeworm life cycle; 1860 Zenker links trichina in pork to human disease; 1880 hookworm anaemia among Gotthard tunnel workers; americas: 1909–1914 – Rockefeller Sanitary Commission campaign against hookworm in the US South
- Read:
  - F. E. G. Cox, History of human parasitology, Clinical Microbiology Reviews (2002)
  - John Ettling, The Germ of Laziness: Rockefeller Philanthropy and Public Health in the New South (1981)
